conventions.rot: forearm rotation in deg: negative = pronation (palm down), positive = supination (palm up), 0 = thumb up
conventions.ext: wrist in deg: positive = extension, negative = flexion
conventions.dev: wrist in deg: positive = ulnar (pinky side), negative = radial (thumb side)
conventions.elbow: elbow flexion in deg (0 = straight, 90 = right angle)
conventions.axial: axial load through the wrist 0..1 (body weight, examiner push)
conventions.force.dir: anatomical direction in the local frame of the bone at the landmark: palmar | dorsal | radial | ulnar | proximal | distal | rotate_pronation | rotate_supination
conventions.landmarks: LM_<id> empties in the glb, see HANDOVER.md 6.3
conventions.hyper: optional extra kinematic offsets shown when the hypermobility toggle is on
conventions.view: camera preset for the test: free | dorsal | thumb | palm | ulnar | end
conventions.risk: 1 = safe to try yourself, 2 = careful: load or a partner involved, 3 = examiner only
conventions.body: per step: posture scene for the mannequin inset: seated_table | seated_elbow_vertical | seated_under_table | chair_press | chair_press_up | standing
conventions.holds: per step: where a second person fixes the limb: forearm | wrist | hand (drawn as a ring)
conventions.sources: per test: where the test is described in the literature (short form, full citation, DOI link, one-line note)
conventions.exercises: per test, optional: exercises from exercises.json that train what the test examines, each with one line saying why. Left out where no exercise fits

globalRules: Always compare with the other side; in a hypermobile wrist only asymmetry or reproducing the usual pain counts.
Gentle, a few repetitions, stop at sharp pain.
A positive test is a hint, not a diagnosis; tests overlap and are often wrong.
Film clunks and snaps for the doctor; they often do not happen on command.

tests.name: Ulnar fovea sign

steps.text: Rest the forearm on a table, thumb up, wrist relaxed.
Press a thumb into the soft spot between the ulnar styloid and the FCU tendon, palm side of the bony bump.

tests.positive: Clear tenderness that reproduces your pain, more than on the other side.
tests.meaning: Points to a foveal TFCC tear or an ulnotriquetral ligament injury.

risk.note: Pressing with a thumb is harmless. Compare both sides.

exercises.why: Works the muscles that press radius and ulna together, without any sliding in the joint.
The next step: the same muscles through a small, slow turn against a light lever.
Steadies the wrist in mid-range; the pinky-side hold works the ECU, which lies right over the TFCC.

sources.cite: Tay SC, Tomita K, Berger RA. The “ulnar fovea sign” for defining ulnar wrist pain: an analysis of sensitivity and specificity. J Hand Surg Am 2007;32(4):438–444.
sources.note: First description of the sign, checked against arthroscopy.

tests.name: Press test

steps.text: Sit on a stable chair, put both palms flat on the seat beside you.
Push yourself up so your body weight goes through the extended wrists.

tests.positive: Pain on the pinky side of the wrist.
tests.home: Exactly as described; stop at the first sharp pain.

risk.note: Your body weight goes through the wrist. Stop at the first sharp pain; skip it while the wrist is acutely painful.

exercises.why: Works the muscles that press radius and ulna together, without any sliding in the joint.
The next step: the same muscles through a small, slow turn against a light lever.
Steadies the wrist in mid-range; the pinky-side hold works the ECU, which lies right over the TFCC.

sources.cite: Lester B, Halbrecht J, Levy IM, Gaudinez R. “Press test” for office diagnosis of triangular fibrocartilage complex tears of the wrist. Ann Plast Surg 1995;35(1):41–45.

tests.name: Ulnocarpal stress test

steps.text: Elbow on the table, forearm vertical; the partner tilts your wrist fully toward the pinky.
The partner pushes the hand down along the forearm axis and turns the forearm palm down ...
... and palm up, keeping the push.

tests.positive: Pain or crepitus on the pinky side.
tests.meaning: TFCC tear, ulnocarpal impaction, LT problems (not specific).
tests.home: Partner does it gently and slowly.

risk.note: A partner pushes and turns the wrist at the end of its range. Slow and gentle only.

exercises.why: Works the muscles that press radius and ulna together, without any sliding in the joint.
The next step: the same muscles through a small, slow turn against a light lever.
Steadies the wrist in mid-range; the pinky-side hold works the ECU, which lies right over the TFCC.

sources.cite: Nakamura R, Horii E, Imaeda T, Nakao E, Kato H, Watanabe K. The ulnocarpal stress test in the diagnosis of ulnar-sided wrist pain. J Hand Surg Br 1997;22(6):719–723.

tests.name: Supination lift test

steps.text: Sit at a heavy table, palms up under its edge, elbows bent 90°.
Try to lift the table.

tests.positive: Pain on the pinky side, or the wrist gives way.

risk.note: Loads the TFCC against a heavy table. Lift gently, never jerk.

exercises.why: Works the muscles that press radius and ulna together, without any sliding in the joint.
The next step: the same muscles through a small, slow turn against a light lever.
Steadies the wrist in mid-range; the pinky-side hold works the ECU, which lies right over the TFCC.

sources.cite: Buterbaugh GA, Brown TR, Horn PC. Ulnar-sided wrist pain in athletes. Clin Sports Med 1998;17(3):567–583.
sources.note: The review this test is usually credited to. Its accuracy has not been studied on its own.

tests.name: DRUJ ballottement / piano key test

steps.text: Neutral forearm. The examiner fixes the radius with one hand and grips the ulnar head between thumb and index of the other.
Shift the ulnar head toward the palm ...
... and toward the back of the hand.
Repeat palm down (piano key: press the prominent ulnar head down; does it spring back?) and palm up.

tests.positive: More translation than on the other side, a soft end point, or pain. Typical for instability: more shift in neutral than at the end of rotation.
tests.meaning: DRUJ instability / laxity of the radioulnar ligaments.
tests.home: Palm down, press the ulnar head toward the palm with the other hand; compare both sides.

risk.note: Home version: gentle pressure on the ulnar head; compare both sides.

exercises.why: Works the muscles that press radius and ulna together, without any sliding in the joint.
The next step: the same muscles through a small, slow turn against a light lever.
Reactive control of the forearm and wrist muscles with a light, unsteady load.

sources.cite: Moriya T, Aoki M, Iba K, Ozasa Y, Wada T, Yamashita T. Effect of triangular ligament tears on distal radioulnar joint instability and evaluation of three clinical tests: a biomechanical study. J Hand Surg Eur 2009;34(2):219–223.
sources.note: Ballottement test compared with other DRUJ tests in the lab.

sources.cite: Onishi T, Omokawa S, Iida A, et al. Biomechanical study of distal radioulnar joint ballottement test. J Orthop Res 2017;35(5):1123–1127.
sources.note: How the hold on the radius and carpus changes the result.

sources.cite: Cooney WP, Linscheid RL, Dobyns JH (eds). The Wrist: Diagnosis and Operative Treatment. St. Louis: Mosby; 1998.
sources.note: Textbook the piano key sign is credited to in later reviews.

tests.name: ECU subluxation test

steps.text: Palm down; rest a finger on the back of the ulnar head.
Turn the palm up while bending the wrist palm-ward and tilting it toward the pinky.

tests.positive: A snap, or the tendon cord jumping sideways over the bump.

risk.note: Harmless, but do not make a snapping tendon snap more than a few times; it irritates the sheath.

sources.cite: Burkhart SS, Wood MB, Linscheid RL. Posttraumatic recurrent subluxation of the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon. J Hand Surg Am 1982;7(1):1–3.
sources.note: Early description of the tendon snapping out in supination, flexion and ulnar deviation.

sources.cite: Campbell D, Campbell R, O’Connor P, Hawkes R. Sports-related extensor carpi ulnaris pathology: a review of functional anatomy, sports injury and management. Br J Sports Med 2013;47(17):1105–1111.
sources.note: Review of ECU anatomy, instability and examination.

tests.name: ECU synergy test

steps.text: Forearm palm up on the table, elbow 90°, fingers straight.
Push the thumb away from the palm (sideways) against the partner's resistance; ECU and FCU co-contract.

tests.positive: Pain along the back of the pinky side (ECU course).
tests.meaning: ECU tendinitis rather than an intra-articular (TFCC) problem.

risk.note: Low load, but a partner has to resist the thumb.

exercises.why: The pinky-side hold loads the ECU tendon without movement, the gentlest way to start with an irritated tendon.
Later: slow lowering work for the wrist extensors, the ECU included, in a small range.

sources.cite: Ruland RT, Hogan CJ. The ECU synergy test: an aid to diagnose ECU tendonitis. J Hand Surg Am 2008;33(10):1777–1782.

tests.name: Midcarpal shift test (Lichtman)

steps.text: Palm down, wrist slightly tilted to the thumb side.
The examiner pushes the hand toward the palm at the level of the carpal bones ...
... then tilts the wrist toward the pinky with slight axial load.

tests.positive: A clunk as the carpus snaps back (proximal row jumps from flexed to extended); grading I–V by Lichtman.
tests.meaning: Palmar midcarpal instability, common in hypermobility.
tests.home: Use the active catch-up clunk test instead.

risk.note: The examiner pushes the carpus into the clunk; forcing it can hurt. At home use the active catch-up clunk instead.

exercises.why: The pinky-side hold works the ECU, one of the muscles that lifts the sagging pinky side of the carpus.
A light grip tightens both muscle groups and presses the two carpal rows together.
Trains the quick, unconscious control that keeps the carpus from slipping into the clunk.

sources.cite: Lichtman DM, Schneider JR, Swafford AR, Mack GR. Ulnar midcarpal instability—clinical and laboratory analysis. J Hand Surg Am 1981;6(5):515–523.
sources.note: First description of the instability and of the test.

sources.cite: Feinstein WK, Lichtman DM, Noble PC, Alexander JW, Hipp JA. Quantitative assessment of the midcarpal shift test. J Hand Surg Am 1999;24(5):977–983.

tests.name: Active catch-up clunk (self test)

steps.text: Palm down, loose fist, wrist tilted to the thumb side, some grip tension.
Slowly tilt to the pinky side.

tests.positive: A visible, often painful clunk midway.

risk.note: A few slow repetitions only; stop if the clunk hurts.

exercises.why: The pinky-side hold works the ECU, one of the muscles that lifts the sagging pinky side of the carpus.
A light grip tightens both muscle groups and presses the two carpal rows together.
Trains the quick, unconscious control that keeps the carpus from slipping into the clunk.

sources.cite: Lichtman DM, Wroten ES. Understanding midcarpal instability. J Hand Surg Am 2006;31(3):491–498.
sources.note: Explains the catch-up clunk on tilting toward the pinky.

sources.cite: Lichtman DM, Schneider JR, Swafford AR, Mack GR. Ulnar midcarpal instability—clinical and laboratory analysis. J Hand Surg Am 1981;6(5):515–523.

tests.name: Watson test (scaphoid shift)

steps.text: Examiner's thumb on the scaphoid tubercle (palm side), wrist tilted to the pinky side.
Move the wrist to the thumb side while pressing the tubercle; the scaphoid wants to flex and is blocked.
Release the thumb.

tests.positive: Pain on the back of the wrist at the SL interval, or a clunk on release.
tests.meaning: Scapholunate instability; also positive in many lax but healthy wrists – compare sides.
tests.home: Not recommended (hard to do on yourself, painful when positive).

risk.note: Painful when positive and hard to do on yourself. Shown so you know what to expect.

exercises.why: Works the thumb-side muscles, which lab studies describe as the ones that steady scaphoid and lunate.
Moves the wrist along the path on which scaphoid and lunate shift least against each other.

sources.cite: Watson HK, Ashmead D 4th, Makhlouf MV. Examination of the scaphoid. J Hand Surg Am 1988;13(5):657–660.
sources.note: First description of the scaphoid shift manoeuvre.

tests.name: LT ballottement (Reagan)

steps.text: The examiner fixes the lunate between thumb and index of one hand, and the triquetrum and pisiform with the other.
Shift the triquetrum up and down against the lunate.

tests.positive: Pain, laxity or crepitus at the LT interval.
tests.home: Only a partner who knows the anatomy (e.g. a doctor).

risk.note: Needs exact knowledge of the anatomy. Shown so you know what to expect.

exercises.why: The pinky-side hold works the ECU, which lab studies describe as the muscle that steadies lunate and triquetrum.

sources.cite: Reagan DS, Linscheid RL, Dobyns JH. Lunotriquetral sprains. J Hand Surg Am 1984;9(4):502–514.

tests.name: Beighton score (general hypermobility)

steps.text: Little finger bends back past 90° (1 point per side).
Thumb can be pulled onto the forearm (1 point per side).
Elbow straightens more than 10° past straight (1 point per side).

textOnly: Knee hyperextends more than 10° (1 point per side).
Palms flat on the floor with straight knees (1 point).
tests.positive: 5 or more of 9 points (adults up to 50; 4 or more above 50) suggests generalised hypermobility.

risk.note: Harmless; do not force any joint past what feels comfortable.

exercises.why: The starting point for a lax wrist: holding steady in mid-range.
The same for the joint between radius and ulna.
A light grip as the wrist's own muscular brace.
Quick, unconscious control, which tends to be weaker in hypermobile joints.

sources.cite: Beighton P, Solomon L, Soskolne CL. Articular mobility in an African population. Ann Rheum Dis 1973;32(5):413–418.
Malfait F, Francomano C, Byers P, et al. The 2017 international classification of the Ehlers–Danlos syndromes. Am J Med Genet C Semin Med Genet 2017;175(1):8–26.
